# Work state: your to-do lists and working state
Use claude-mem's work_state_write tool to track all to-do lists and multi-step work. It is your canonical to-do list: use it instead of any built-in to-do tool. Also use it to track the state of anything you need an ongoing understanding of. Whatever is still open is shown here at the start of every session in this project.
- One list per to-do list or tracked thing: work_state_write with list="<name>" and the fields to set
- To-do item: fields {"task": "<name>", "status": "todo" | "doing" | "done" | "dropped", ...any details}
- State: fields {"<key>": <value>} (the latest value of each key wins; null clears a key; "status": "done" closes the list)
- Made something a person can open (PR, deck, page, image, report)? Attach it to that item: fields {"work_product": "https://…" or "/absolute/file"}; several, with titles, as one JSON string: "[{\"title\": \"<name>\", \"url\": \"https://…\"}]"
- Deliverables: write a deck, report, page or other file the person asked for as a file and attach it as work_product before you finish. When you stop, claude-mem copies each attached file (and any deck, document, page, image or spreadsheet you wrote outside the source tree) into this project's deliverables bucket, ~/.claude-mem/deliverables/<project>/, and links it on the request's card in My Work.
- Read every list, closed items included: work_state_read with includeClosed=true

S3 Add pause(tag) and resume(tag) to the schedule library so tagged jobs can be suspended during maintenance windows without cancelling and re-adding them, with tests (Nov 3, 7:13 PM)
**Investigated**: The Scheduler job-selection path in schedule/__init__.py: run_pending filters on Job.should_run, run_all ignores should_run, get_next_run and idle_seconds read next_run across all tagged jobs, and Job.should_run compares only the current time to next_run. The existing tag-based get_jobs and clear methods, the module-level wrappers, the test file conventions, and the docs/reference.rst autofunction list were also examined.

**Learned**: Because should_run compares only against next_run, a job skipped while paused keeps a past next_run and runs once on the first run_pending after resume. run_all bypasses should_run entirely, so pause needed an explicit decision there. Without excluding paused jobs from get_next_run and idle_seconds, a paused overdue job would give a negative idle_seconds and could make a sleep loop spin.

**Completed**: Added Scheduler.pause(tag) and Scheduler.resume(tag), backed by a _paused_tags set initialized in __init__. run_pending skips any job with a paused tag, including multi-tag jobs where any tag is paused. get_next_run, next_run and idle_seconds ignore paused jobs and return None when all matching jobs are paused. clear(tag) un-pauses that tag, and clear() empties the pause set. Module-level pause and resume wrappers were added, and docs/reference.rst gained autofunction entries for both. Five tests were added to test_schedule.py covering tag pause and resume, jobs added later, multi-tag jobs, unknown and repeated resume calls, next_run/idle_seconds/run_all with paused jobs, and clear resetting pause. The full suite passes with 88 tests. Changes are in three modified files and are not committed.

**Next Steps**: Commit the pause/resume changes to schedule/__init__.py, test_schedule.py, and docs/reference.rst. Build the autoclass docs to confirm the new pause and resume entries render. Await the user's decision on whether run_all should respect paused tags, since it currently still runs them.

**Notes**: A design choice in the pause semantics needs confirmation: run_all still runs paused jobs, which the docstring documents as intentional. The rationale given was that run_all means "run everything now", but this could surprise maintenance-window users. Pausing also applies to jobs tagged after the pause call, which the user has not explicitly confirmed. The earlier commit a5d1ad4 for get_jobs_for is the most recent committed work, and this pause/resume work sits on top of it uncommitted.
